keyConcepts.title: Client-server vs. P2P
keyConcepts.text: Client-server relies on always-on servers with fixed addresses. P2P lets peers talk directly and is **self-scaling**: each new peer adds capacity as well as demand.

keyConcepts.title: Sockets and addressing
keyConcepts.text: A process sends and receives through a **socket**. To reach a process you need the host's **IP address** and the process's **port number** (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25, DNS 53).

keyConcepts.title: TCP vs. UDP services
keyConcepts.text: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and congestion-controlled. UDP is connectionless and unreliable but lightweight. Neither guarantees timing or throughput; TLS adds security on top of TCP.

keyConcepts.title: HTTP is stateless
keyConcepts.text: Servers keep no memory of past requests. **Cookies** add state. Non-persistent HTTP costs about **2 RTT + transmission time** per object; persistent HTTP reuses one connection.

keyConcepts.title: Web caching and conditional GET
keyConcepts.text: Proxy caches answer requests locally to cut delay and access-link traffic. **If-modified-since** checks freshness; **304 Not Modified** means the cached copy is still good.

keyConcepts.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
keyConcepts.text: HTTP/2 splits messages into frames and interleaves them on one TCP connection to avoid head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 runs over **QUIC** (on UDP).

keyConcepts.title: Email: SMTP and IMAP
keyConcepts.text: SMTP **pushes** mail from the sender's server directly to the receiver's server over TCP port 25. Users retrieve mail with **IMAP** or over HTTP (webmail).

keyConcepts.title: DNS hierarchy
keyConcepts.text: Root → TLD → authoritative servers, with a **local DNS server** acting as proxy. Lookups are cached, and records are A, NS, CNAME and MX. DNS runs over UDP port 53.

keyConcepts.title: BitTorrent
keyConcepts.text: Files are split into chunks shared among peers in a torrent. Peers request **rarest first** and upload to their top 4 partners (**tit-for-tat**), plus an optimistic unchoke.

keyConcepts.title: DASH and CDNs
keyConcepts.text: DASH clients pick a bit rate for each chunk based on bandwidth. CDNs copy content to servers near users (**enter deep** or **bring home**) and redirect requests using DNS.

keyConcepts.title: Socket programming
keyConcepts.text: UDP: no connection, and every packet carries the destination address. TCP: handshake first, then a reliable byte stream, with the server creating a new socket per client.

flashcards.back: An always-on server with a fixed IP address serves many clients; clients don't talk to each other directly.
Each new peer adds upload capacity as well as demand, so P2P systems scale as they grow.
The interface (door) between an application process and the transport layer.

flashcards.front: Two things needed to address a process
flashcards.back: The host's IP address and the process's port number.
HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25, DNS 53.
Encryption, data integrity and end-point authentication on top of TCP, implemented in the application.
The server keeps no information about past client requests.
Round-trip time: how long a small packet takes to go from client to server and back.

flashcards.front: Response time for non-persistent HTTP (one object)
flashcards.back: About **2 RTT + file transmission time** (one RTT for the TCP handshake, one for the request/response).
The server leaves the TCP connection open so later requests reuse it. It's the default in HTTP/1.1.

flashcards.front: Four parts of the cookie system
flashcards.back: A Set-cookie header in the response, a Cookie header in later requests, a cookie file on the user's computer, and a back-end database at the site.

flashcards.front: What does a web cache (proxy) do?
flashcards.back: Answers HTTP requests for the origin server using stored copies, cutting response time and access-link traffic.
A request with an If-modified-since header. The server replies 304 Not Modified (empty body) if the object hasn't changed.
Not Found: the requested document doesn't exist on the server.
Moved Permanently: the new URL is in the Location header.
A large object at the front of the connection delays the small objects behind it. HTTP/2 fixes this by interleaving frames.
SMTP pushes mail from the sending server to the receiving server; HTTP users pull information from servers.

flashcards.front: Which protocol retrieves mail from a server?
flashcards.back: IMAP (or HTTP for webmail and apps). SMTP is only for sending.
Translating hostnames (like www.google.com) into IP addresses.

flashcards.front: Order of DNS servers in a lookup
flashcards.back: Local DNS server → root server → TLD server → authoritative server.
Maps a hostname to an IP address.

flashcards.front: DNS record types NS, CNAME and MX
flashcards.back: NS: authoritative server for a domain. CNAME: canonical name for an alias. MX: mail server for a domain.
**max{ NF/u_s , F/d_min }**, which grows linearly with N.
A peer requests the chunks that are rarest among its neighbors first, so rare chunks spread quickly.
A peer uploads to the 4 neighbors sending to it fastest (unchoked), reevaluated every 10 s, plus one random optimistic unchoke every 30 s.
Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP. Video is stored at several bit rates in chunks, and the client picks the rate for each chunk using a manifest file.

flashcards.front: CDN: enter deep vs. bring home
flashcards.back: Enter deep puts many small clusters inside access ISPs (Akamai). Bring home puts fewer big clusters at IXPs (Limelight).

flashcards.front: Python UDP vs. TCP socket types
flashcards.back: UDP: SOCK_DGRAM. TCP: SOCK_STREAM.

flashcards.front: TCP welcoming socket vs. connection socket
flashcards.back: The welcoming socket waits for new clients. accept() creates a separate connection socket for each client.

quiz.q: Which transport service does UDP provide?
quiz.explain: UDP is a no-frills protocol: it delivers to the right process and checks for errors, but it's unreliable and has no congestion control.

quiz.q: With non-persistent HTTP, about how long does it take to fetch one small object (ignoring transmission time)?
quiz.explain: One RTT to set up the TCP connection and one RTT for the request and the start of the response.

quiz.q: What does a 304 Not Modified response mean?
options: The cached copy is still up to date
The object moved to a new URL
The server couldn't find the object
quiz.explain: It's the reply to a conditional GET when the object hasn't changed since the If-modified-since date, so no body is sent.

quiz.q: How do websites keep track of users when HTTP is stateless?
quiz.explain: The site sends a Set-cookie ID; the browser returns it in a Cookie header on later requests.

quiz.q: Which problem does HTTP/2 mainly fix?
options: Head-of-line blocking of small objects behind large ones
quiz.explain: HTTP/2 splits responses into frames and interleaves them on one connection so small objects aren't stuck behind big ones.

quiz.q: Which protocol do mail servers use to send mail to each other?
quiz.explain: SMTP pushes mail between mail servers over TCP port 25. IMAP is for retrieving mail.

quiz.q: In a typical DNS lookup, which server does the local DNS server ask first (with nothing cached)?
quiz.explain: Root servers point to TLD servers, which point to the authoritative server for the domain.

quiz.q: Which DNS record type gives the mail server for a domain?
quiz.explain: MX records give the canonical name of a domain's mail server.

quiz.q: Why does P2P file distribution scale better than client-server?
options: Each new peer adds upload capacity
P2P uses UDP instead of TCP
There's no server involved at all
quiz.explain: In client-server, the server must upload N copies. In P2P, peers upload to each other, so total capacity grows with the number of peers.

quiz.q: In BitTorrent, which chunks does a peer request first?
options: The rarest chunks among its neighbors
The first chunks of the file
quiz.explain: Rarest first spreads rare chunks quickly and keeps the number of copies even across the torrent.

quiz.q: In DASH, who decides which bit rate to request for each chunk?
quiz.explain: The client measures its bandwidth and buffer, then requests each chunk at a suitable bit rate from the manifest.

quiz.q: How do CDNs usually send a user to a nearby server?
quiz.explain: The content provider's DNS server returns a hostname in the CDN's domain, and the CDN's DNS picks a suitable server.

quiz.q: In a TCP server, what does accept() return?
options: A new connection socket dedicated to that client
quiz.explain: The welcoming socket keeps listening, and each client gets its own connection socket.

quiz.q: Which is true of UDP sockets?
options: Every packet must include the destination address and port
A handshake is required before sending
Data arrives as a reliable byte stream
The server makes a new socket per client
quiz.explain: UDP is connectionless, so sendto() includes the destination with each packet.
